paragraphs: It may perhaps be argued that, in place of OCCASIONAL appeals to the people, which are open to the objections urged against them, PERIODICAL appeals are the proper and adequate means of PREVENTING AND CORRECTING INFRACTIONS OF THE CONSTITUTION.

Note that in examining these expedients I confine myself to how well they would ENFORCE the Constitution by keeping the separate departments of power within their proper bounds. I am not considering them in particular as ways of ALTERING the Constitution itself. Looked at in the first way, appeals to the people at fixed periods seem almost as unsuitable as appeals on particular occasions, as these arise. Suppose the periods are separated by short intervals. Then the measures to be reviewed and corrected will be recent, and will be tangled up with all the circumstances that tend to corrupt and distort the result of occasional revisions. Suppose the periods are far apart. Then the same remark applies to all recent measures. And whatever advantage the distance of the older measures may give to a dispassionate review of them comes with drawbacks that seem to outweigh it. In the first place, a distant prospect of public censure would be a very feeble restraint on power when present motives drive it to excess. Can anyone imagine that a legislative assembly of a hundred or two hundred members, eagerly bent on some favorite object and breaking through the restraints of the Constitution to reach it, would be stopped by the thought that its conduct would be reviewed by a censorial body ten, fifteen or twenty years from now? In the next place, the abuses would often have done their harm before the remedy was applied. And in the last place, where that might not be so, the abuses would be of long standing, would have taken deep root, and would not easily be pulled out.

The scheme of revising the constitution, in order to correct recent breaches of it as well as for other purposes, has actually been tried in one of the States. One of the tasks of the Council of Censors that met in Pennsylvania in 1783 and 1784 was, as we have seen, to inquire "whether the constitution had been violated, and whether the legislative and executive departments had encroached upon each other." This important and novel experiment in politics deserves very particular attention from several points of view. In some respects, as a single experiment made under somewhat peculiar circumstances, it may perhaps be thought not absolutely conclusive. But as applied to the case under consideration, it involves some facts that I venture to say are a complete and satisfactory illustration of the reasoning I have used.

First. The names of the gentlemen who made up the council show that some of its most active members, at least, had also been active and leading figures in the parties that already existed in the State.

Second. The same active and leading members of the council had, it appears, been active and influential members of the legislative and executive branches during the very period under review. Some had even been patrons or opponents of the measures that were now to be tested against the constitution. Two of the members had been vice-presidents of the State, and several others members of the executive council, in the seven preceding years. One of them had been speaker, and a number of others distinguished members, of the legislative assembly in the same period.

Third. Every page of the council's proceedings shows what these circumstances did to the temper of its deliberations. For as long as the council lasted, it was split into two fixed and violent parties. The members themselves acknowledged and lamented the fact. Even if they had not, the record of their proceedings gives equally satisfactory proof. On every question, however unimportant in itself or unconnected with the others, the same names stand opposed in the opposite columns. Any unbiased observer may infer, without risk of mistake and without meaning to reflect on either party or on any individual in either, that, unfortunately, PASSION, not REASON, must have presided over their decisions. When men use their reason coolly and freely on a variety of distinct questions, they inevitably come to different opinions on some of them. When they are ruled by a common passion, their opinions, if they can be called that, will be the same.

Fourth. It is at least doubtful whether, in several instances, this body's decisions misconstrue the limits prescribed for the legislative and executive departments, rather than holding those departments to their constitutional places.

Fifth. As far as I have understood, the council's decisions on constitutional questions, whether rightly or wrongly reached, have had no effect in changing the practice that rests on legislative constructions. It even appears, if I am not mistaken, that in one instance the legislature of the day rejected the council's constructions and in fact won the contest.
This censorial body, therefore, proves at once, through its investigations, that the disease exists, and, through its own example, that the remedy is ineffective.

It cannot be argued against this conclusion that the State where the experiment was made was at that moment, and had long been, violently heated and torn by the rage of party. Are we to presume that at any future seven-year point the same State will be free from parties? Are we to presume that any other State, at that point or any other, will be exempt from them? Such a thing ought to be neither presumed nor desired, because the end of parties necessarily means either a universal alarm for the public safety or the complete end of liberty.

Suppose a precaution were taken to exclude from the assemblies elected by the people to review the previous administration of the government everyone who had had any connection with the government during the period in question. The difficulties would still not be removed. The important task would probably fall to men who, with lesser abilities, would be little better qualified in other respects. They might not have been personally involved in the administration, and so might not have been direct agents in the measures to be examined. But they would probably have been caught up in the parties tied to those measures, and would have been elected under their auspices.
